newsitem.title: USA: Economic strength again drives U.S. stocks, bonds lower.
newsitem.headline: Economic strength again drives U.S. stocks, bonds lower.

text.p: Stock and bond prices fell for the second straight session Friday after reports of surprising strength in the economy reinforced worries the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in a bid to ward off inflation.
But the reports helped the dollar, which rose against most major currencies. Gold prices fell and crude oil edged higher.

The Dow Jones industrial average lost 31.44 points to close at 5,616.21 after falling nearly 65 points on Thursday. For the week, the 30-share index lost 106.53 points, its worst performance since the last week of May.
Volume of 256 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange was the lowest full session of the year. In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 1,469 to 802.

Bond prices also fell. The 30-year Treasury lost almost a point, raising its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, to 7.12 percent from 7.04 percent late Thursday. The 30-year bond fell about three-quarters of a point on Thursday.
Friday's sell-off was sparked by reports of strong factory orders in July and a sharp jump in a survey of manufacturing by Chicago area purchasing managers.
"The Chicago PMI number today was very ugly," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management. "That seemed to be the catalyst."
The Chicago group said its Purchasing Managers Index, a gauge of manufacturing in the region, jumped to 60 in August from 51.2 in July. A reading above 50 indicates growth.
Separately, the Commerce Department said orders for manufactured goods climbed 1.8 percent in July to a seasonally adjusted $317.6 billion -- nearly twice the increase that had been expected.

The reports fanned worries on Wall Street that the Fed, the nation's central bank, would raise rates next month in a bid to ward off inflation. Higher rates tend to slow the economy and hurt corporate earnings, thus depressing stocks.
The reports, coupled with Thursday's upward revision of second-quarter economic growth, shook markets that had largely dismissed the possibility of a rise in rates before the November elections.
"Until these last reports, almost no one thought the evidence would be that overwhelming," said Robert Stovall, president of Stovall/21st Advisors.
Analysts said that while the trading activity may recover after Labour Day, market jitters are likely to persist.

"Next week should be a much better test for volume, but the market is still one day bullish and one day bearish," said Marshall Acuff, portfolio manager at Smith Barney. "Until they can figure out what's going on (in the economy), I don't see that being resolved quickly," he said.

The dollar rose to 1.4820 German marks, up from 1.4770 Thursday, and to 108.90 Japanese yen from 108.42, boosted by the growing perception that German rates will keep falling while American rates are likely to rise. Higher American rates tend to make dollar-based investments more attractive, while lower German rates would do the reverse for investments in marks.
The sell-off in stock and bond prices tempered the dollar's gains, traders said.
In commodity markets, gold for December delivery fell $1.10 to $391.30 an ounce at New York's Commodity Exchange, after touching $390, its lowest in nearly a month.
October crude oil rose 10 cents to $22.25 a barrel at the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 fell 17.4 points to 3,867.7 and the 225-share Nikkei average in Tokyo lost 386.26 points, or 1.88 percent, to close at 20,166.90.
